subject: paediatrics
title: Primary Dentition, Dental Milestones and Parental Height

steps.tx: The initial set of twenty deciduous teeth constitutes **primary milk dentition**, comprising eight incisors, four canines, and eight molars. Unlike the permanent dentition, premolars are completely absent in the primary set. Eruption follows a predictable chronological sequence beginning in the sixth to eighth month of life, with all primary teeth erupting by thirty months.
steps.say: Primary dentition comprises twenty teeth, completely lacking premolars, and finishes by thirty months.

vis.alt: Anatomical dental charts showing primary and permanent teeth eruption.
vis.caption: Anatomical eruption sequence of primary deciduous teeth and permanent dentition. [Credit: StewardMD]

steps.tx: The very first teeth to erupt into the oral cavity are the **mandibular central incisors**, appearing between six and eight months of age. These are followed sequentially by the maxillary central incisors at eight to ten months, maxillary and mandibular lateral incisors at ten to twelve months, first molars at twelve to sixteen months, canines at sixteen to twenty months, and second molars at twenty to thirty months.
steps.say: Mandibular central incisors erupt first around six months, followed by maxillary central incisors.

steps.tx: A convenient clinical rule of thumb estimates expected tooth numbers in infants using the **age in months minus six rule**. For example, a healthy twelve-month-old infant is expected to have six erupted deciduous incisors. Calcification of primary teeth begins during the fourteenth to sixteenth week of intrauterine fetal life, making maternal nutrition and medications like tetracyclines critical determinants of enamel health.
steps.say: The number of primary teeth roughly equals the child's age in months minus six up to two years.

left.title: Rule of Thumb Formula
points: Number of erupted teeth = Age in months - 6
Valid up to 24 months of age

right.title: Enamel Vulnerability
points: In utero calcification begins at 14 weeks
Severe systemic illness creates enamel hypoplasia

steps.tx: The failure of any primary tooth to erupt by thirteen months of age defines **pathological delayed dentition**. While constitutional or familial delay is the most common benign etiology, delayed eruption frequently serves as a sensitive clinical sign of underlying endocrine or metabolic disorders, notably congenital hypothyroidism, nutritional rickets, hypopituitarism, and cleidocranial dysplasia.
steps.say: Delayed dentition is the absence of teeth by thirteen months, pointing toward rickets or hypothyroidism.

rows: Vitamin D deficiency and impaired mineralisation
RUNX2 gene mutation affecting bone remodeling
Upward slanting palpebral fissures, flat profile

steps.tx: Transition to the permanent dentition begins at six years of age with eruption of the **first permanent six-year molar**. Crucially, the first permanent molar erupts posterior to the second deciduous molar without shedding any primary tooth. Permanent incisors subsequently erupt between six and eight years as deciduous incisors are shed.
steps.say: The first permanent molar erupts at six years behind primary teeth without shedding a baby tooth.

left.title: Six-Year Permanent Molar
points: Erupts directly posterior to deciduous molars
Does not replace an existing primary tooth

right.title: Shedding of Deciduous Teeth
points: Begins with mandibular central incisors at 6 years
Continues sequentially through 12 years of age

steps.tx: Predicting an individual child's adult height genetic potential utilizes the **mid-parental target height calculation**. Because adult stature is a polygenic trait inherited equally from both biological parents, the formula adjusts for the thirteen-centimeter biological height difference between adult males and females, establishing an expected genetic target range.
steps.say: The mid-parental height formula establishes expected genetic target stature adjusted for sex.

steps.tx: Clinical assessment of dental health requires identifying **early childhood caries**, previously designated nursing bottle caries. Prolonged nocturnal bottle feeding with milk, fruit juices, or sweetened liquids allows fermentable carbohydrates to pool around maxillary incisors, where Streptococcus mutans generates acid that rapidly demineralizes enamel, characteristically sparing mandibular incisors protected by the tongue.
steps.say: Nursing caries destroys maxillary incisors from pooling nocturnal milk, sparing lower teeth.

left.title: Severe Maxillary Involvement
points: Maxillary central and lateral incisors decayed

right.title: Mandibular Incisor Sparing
points: Protected by tongue posture during suckling

steps.tx: Routine pediatric preventative oral health care mandates **fluoride toothpaste and dental visits**. Tooth brushing should commence as soon as the first deciduous tooth erupts, using a tiny rice-grain smear of fluoridated toothpaste for children under three years of age, expanding to a pea-sized amount for children aged three to six years, accompanied by dental checks.
steps.say: Brushing starts with the first tooth using a rice-grain smear of fluoride toothpaste under age three.

rows: Minimizes systemic swallowing and fluorosis risk
